chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hisham ibn Salim and Muhammad ibn Humran from al-Walid ibn Sabih, who said:

I entered upon Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), and Zurarah was coming out from his presence. Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to me, 'O Walid, do you not wonder at Zururah? He asked me about the actions of these people. What did he want me to say to him, 'No,' so he would narrate that to me?' Then he said, 'O Walid, when did the Shia begin to ask about their actions? The Shia used to say,

key_terms.زُرَارَة: Zururah, a prominent companion of the Imams

ai.seo_question: What does the Imam mean when he says the Shia used to just eat the Imams' food and rest in their shade?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights the transition of the Shia community from a period of informal, intimate reliance on the Imam’s physical presence and sustenance to a more formalized era of seeking specific legal rulings (*ahkam*). Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) uses this historical shift to contextualize Zurarah’s inquiry, suggesting that the question about 'these people's actions' was not merely about legal detail but served as a strategic test to establish authoritative precedent. This reflects the broader scholarly evolution in Shia jurisprudence where the Imam’s role expanded from spiritual guide to legislative authority.
